explained.validators.hardware.meta.title: Validator hardware: what to run a 6529 validator on
explained.validators.hardware.meta.descr: Home and office tiers first, then datacenter and cloud options with instance types and prices at nine providers, your own Ethereum node, and how large TDH holders run several machines.
explained.validators.hardware.title: Validator hardware
explained.validators.hardware.source.ref: read by hand on the day shown, and checked again for each release
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.in: Answer two or three questions for one suggestion. In the test phase, any machine works.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.wh: Can you keep a machine running at home or at your office?
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.no: Will you also run your own Ethereum node?
You don't need one. The validator checks every answer it gets from any Ethereum server.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.sp: Do you have a computer you can leave on all day?
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.ac: Start with the computer you have.
If it has {cores} and {ram} of memory, it is enough. Turn off sleep, and plug in a network cable if you can.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.go: A small computer on wired Ethernet, with a small UPS. It draws about {watts} and costs about {month} a month over four years, power included.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.gr: Run a home server with its own Ethereum node.
Your validator then reads Ethereum from a node you run. Plan on {ram} of memory and a {disk} NVMe drive, about {buy} in all.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.ra: A dedicated server with unmetered traffic runs the validator and an Ethereum node for {month} a month. A big cloud charges {cloud} a month for the same job.
explained.validators.hardware.chooser.cl: Any VM with {vcpu} and {ram} of memory works, for {month} a month. If you can run a machine at home or at work later, it helps the network more.
explained.validators.hardware.home.why: Why home and office come first
explained.validators.hardware.home.sprea: Validators at home sit in many places, behind many internet providers. Cloud VMs gather in a few companies' buildings. One of the network's goals is that no single hosting company or internet provider carries more than a third of the validators' weight.
explained.validators.hardware.home.priva: At home the validator opens no port and sends its traffic through Tor, so peers and Ethereum servers don't see your address. A cloud VM is tied to a billing account.
explained.validators.hardware.home.cost: A Good mini PC costs about {good} a month over four years, power included. That matches the cheapest small hosts. The cheapest VM at AWS, Google Cloud or Azure costs about {cloud} a month.
explained.validators.hardware.tier.accep: power only, or about {month} a month for a new Pi
explained.validators.hardware.tier.basis: Prices read {date}. Power at {kwh} a kWh, the US average for August.
explained.validators.hardware.dc.intro: If you can't keep a machine at home or at work, a datacenter is a fine place for a validator. It is also a good place for a second machine.
explained.validators.hardware.dc.rackCos: rented with its own Ethereum node, or your own hardware in a colocation rack
explained.validators.hardware.dc.cloudCo: data you download is free at every provider

explained.validators.hardware.cloud.tipA: Arm types cost less at AWS and Azure, and the validator has an Arm build for Linux.
explained.validators.hardware.cloud.tipB: Burstable types are fine. The validator works a few minutes a day, so its daily average stays far below their baseline.
explained.validators.hardware.cloud.tipS: Pick a provider and a country where fewer validators run, and don't put all your machines with one company.
explained.validators.hardware.node.label: Your own node
explained.validators.hardware.node.title: Running your own Ethereum node
explained.validators.hardware.node.p1: You don't need one. Any Ethereum server works, because the validator checks every answer against Ethereum's own block headers. A server can be slow or stop answering, but it can't make your validator sign a wrong result.
explained.validators.hardware.node.p2: A node of your own keeps your Ethereum reads private and adds a data source that no company runs. It needs far more than the validator does.
explained.validators.hardware.node.stora: {disk} of TLC NVMe with DRAM. A full node's database is {db} today, and ethereum.org expects {small} to be too small by {by}. Network disks are too slow.
explained.validators.hardware.node.inter: {down} down and {up} up. The node sends about {upload} a month to its peers, as 6529's own node measured.
explained.validators.hardware.node.softw: An execution client and a consensus client. The consensus client adds {consensus} of disk.
explained.validators.hardware.node.growt: The database keeps growing. The latest published rates are from {year}, at half of today's gas limit, so expect faster growth now.

explained.validators.hardware.node.note: The local NVMe of the AWS and Azure types is wiped when the instance stops. Hetzner's smallest AX servers have too little disk as sold. Google Cloud was not priced for a node.
explained.validators.hardware.holders.ti: Setting up several machines under one account
explained.validators.hardware.holders.gr: One grant from your wallet lists up to {keys} keys, each with its own share of your weight. Give the most reliable machine the largest share.
explained.validators.hardware.holders.do: While one machine is down, the others still sign their shares. Your account stays registered as long as any of its keys signs within seven days.
explained.validators.hardware.holders.ba: A backup is another key in the grant, never a copy of a key. Restoring a copied key on a day its old machine already signed is a double vote, and it excludes your whole account.
explained.validators.hardware.holders.wa: Sign the grant from a cold or hardware wallet. At home, keep Tor on and publish no location.
explained.validators.hardware.holders.sp: Splitting your holdings into several accounts lowers your TDH, because sets and boosts count once per identity. It earns nothing either: this release pays nothing.

explained.validators.hardware.faq.label: Questions
explained.validators.hardware.faq.title: Questions operators ask
explained.validators.hardware.faq.off.q: Can I turn the machine off at night?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.off.a: Yes, as long as it is on long enough inside the signing window, about {open} to {close} each day, to finish its daily run. Your account stays registered for seven days without a signature. This release has no penalty for being offline; the only fault is signing twice.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.node.q: Do I need my own Ethereum node?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.node.a: No. Your validator checks every answer from any Ethereum server against Ethereum's block headers, with its own light client. A server can be slow, but it can't make your validator sign a wrong result.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.eth.q: Do I need ETH, or to stake anything?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.eth.a: No. Nothing is staked at any tier. The Great tier runs an Ethereum node, not an Ethereum validator.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.intern: How much of my internet will it use?
About {wire} a month from the default servers. That fits almost any home plan. It matters only on a metered or satellite link.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.addres: Will other people see my home address?
Not with the defaults. At home the validator only connects out, opens no port, and sends everything through its built-in Tor client, Ethereum calls included.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.pi.q: Can I use a Raspberry Pi?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.pi.a: Yes, one with {ram} of memory. Use the {os}, and boot from an SSD rather than an SD card.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.os.q: Can I run it on a Mac or a Windows PC?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.os.a: Yes: {mac}, or {windows}. Set the computer never to sleep, or it misses its signing window.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.wifi.q: Is Wi-Fi fine, or do I need a cable?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.wifi.a: Wi-Fi works. A cable drops less often, which is why the Good tier asks for one.
Which cloud provider should I pick?
Any of them works. Arm types cost less at AWS and Azure. To spread the network, pick a provider and a country where fewer validators run.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.oracle: For the test phase, yes: {free}, free. Since {halved} it is half its old size. Oracle may also reclaim an idle free instance, and a validator looks idle by its measures. For a validator meant to stay up, upgrade the account to pay-as-you-go, where free resources stay free.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.bill.q: Will my cloud bill include the Ethereum data?
explained.validators.hardware.faq.bill.a: No. Clouds charge for data going out, and almost all of a validator's data comes in. Its own upload is a few GB a month, an estimate not yet measured.
explained.validators.hardware.faq.shared: Can two accounts share one machine?
Yes. Each account has its own keys, and each key still runs on one machine only. Both go offline together when the machine does.
